idiom_name: iterator method with yield return (compiler-generated IEnumerator<T>)
implementation_notes: The Iterator/ConcreteIterator pair is replaced by the compiler: a method returning IEnumerable<T> that uses yield return becomes a generated state machine implementing IEnumerator<T>, and foreach expands to GetEnumerator()/MoveNext()/Current with Dispose in a finally block, so no cursor class is written by hand. Implement IEnumerable<T>/IEnumerator<T> manually only when you need a struct enumerator (to avoid per-loop allocation), extra cursor operations, or a type that is its own enumerator; the compiler-generated enumerator is a class instance per GetEnumerator() call.
pitfalls: Iterators are deferred: calling the method runs no code until the first MoveNext(), so argument validation is skipped unless the method is split into a validating wrapper and a private iterator that yields.

Enumerator state is not thread-safe and List/Dictionary enumerators throw InvalidOperationException when the collection is modified during the loop (versioning); snapshot with ToList() when the body mutates the source.

yield is forbidden in try blocks with catch (and in unsafe blocks before C# 13), and cleanup depends on the finally/Dispose path - it only runs if the consumer disposes, which foreach does but a manually driven enumerator may not.
IAsyncEnumerable<T>/await foreach is the asynchronous counterpart; wrapping blocking IO in a synchronous iterator freezes the caller instead of suspending it.

variants.name: LINQ deferred query pipelines
variants.idiom_name: IEnumerable<T> operator chains (Where/Select/OrderBy) with deferred execution
variants.implementation_notes: LINQ expresses traversal as a lazy pipeline of standard query operators over IEnumerable<T>: Where/Select/OrderBy each return a new enumerable, and nothing executes until a foreach or a terminal operator (ToList/Count/First) enumerates the chain - streaming operators yield per element while nonstreaming ones (OrderBy, GroupBy) buffer the whole source first. This replaces hand-written iterator classes for filter/transform/join work; drop back to yield-based iterators or a custom IEnumerator<T> for stateful traversals the operators cannot express.
variants.code_sketch:
var report = orders
    .Where(o => o.IsPending)
    .OrderBy(o => o.Total)
    .Select(o => new { o.Id, o.Total });
foreach (var row in report) Print(row);   // one lazy chain; executes here
pitfalls: Deferred pipelines re-execute on every enumeration, so an expensive or non-deterministic source is re-queried unless the result is materialized once (ToList); the query also observes mutations made after it was declared.
Nonstreaming operators (OrderBy, GroupBy, Reverse) read and buffer the entire input before producing the first element, destroying the streaming benefit exactly where it was assumed.

Some operators are immediate (Count, Any, First) and some deferred, and the difference is not visible in the call chain - a pipeline that ends in an immediate operator runs once, one that ends in Select runs per enumeration.
